q: The Profiler shows that OrderRow rendered 5,000 times during one keystroke. How do you make React DevTools tell you why each row rendered?
options: Wrap each row in <StrictMode>, which logs the cause of every render
Tick "Record why each component rendered while profiling", then record again
Log the props in the row and compare them by hand
Switch to a production build, where the Profiler names the cause of each commit
explain: The Profiler setting "Record why each component rendered while profiling" adds a "Why did this render?" section to the selected component, with reasons such as "The parent component rendered." or "Props changed:". StrictMode only double-calls render functions to expose impure code; it explains nothing about causes.

q: Which of these does not, on its own, make a component render?
options: Its parent component rendered, with identical props
A context that the component reads received a new value
A prop object was mutated in place
A custom hook it calls updated a state variable it holds
explain: React renders a component when its state (including a hook's state) changes, when its parent renders, or when a context it reads changes. Mutating an object does not notify React at all, which is why mutation leads to stale UI. "Parent rendered" is the tempting wrong answer, but it is precisely the default cause: React renders all children of a rendering component.

q: The page keeps isColumnMenuOpen in OrdersPage, which also renders the 5,000-row table. What is the cheapest change that stops the table from rendering when the menu opens?
options: Move the open state into a ColumnMenu component
Wrap setColumnMenuOpen in useCallback so the table gets a stable setter
Store the open state in a ref instead
Wrap OrdersPage in memo so its children skip the render
explain: With the state inside ColumnMenu, toggling it renders the menu only, and OrdersPage has no state left to re-render the table: no memoization needed. Wrapping OrdersPage in memo is the tempting answer, but memo only skips renders caused by the parent, never by the component's own state; and a ref would not update the UI at all.

q: How does memo decide to skip a render?
options: It deep-compares the old and new props, recursively
It compares the rendered output of the last render with the new one
It skips when the parent rendered for a reason unrelated to this child
It compares each prop with Object.is and skips when all are equal
explain: By default memo compares each prop with Object.is, a shallow comparison: equal primitives match, but two different objects with the same content do not. React never deep-compares props by default, and comparing rendered output would require rendering, which is what memo avoids.

q: OrderSummary is cheap; MemoPanel is wrapped in memo. Each keystroke renders OrdersPage. Does MemoPanel render?
options: No: none of its props depends on query
No: memo leaves children out of its comparison, since they are only elements
Yes: children is a new element object on every render
Only in development, because of StrictMode
explain: JSX creates a new element object on every render, and children is an ordinary prop, so Object.is sees a change each time: measured on React 19.3.1, the memoized wrapper and its child rendered after one keystroke. React has no special case that ignores children; memoize the element or let the compiler do it.

q: Rows are memoized and keyed by array index. A new order arrives and is inserted at the top of the 5,000 orders. How many existing rows render?
options: All of them: every index now holds a different order
None: a memoized row renders only when its own order object changes
Only the last row
One: React detects the insertion and shifts the existing rows
explain: With key={index}, the row at position 0 now receives the new order, the row at position 1 the former first order, and so on: every row's order prop changed. Measured on React 19.3.1: 5,001 renders with index keys, 1 with key={order.id}. React cannot detect an insertion without stable keys.

q: Each memoized row calls useContext(BackOfficeContext) to read selectedOrderId. The provider value also holds query. What happens to the rows on a keystroke?
options: None: memo stops renders while the row's own props are unchanged
Only the rows matching the new query
Each row renders, but React skips its commit, so it costs nothing
Every row renders: every reader of a changed context does
explain: When the provider's value changes, React re-renders every component that reads that context, and react.dev states that memo does not prevent it. Measured: 5,000 row renders per keystroke until the query moved to its own context. Renders are not free just because the DOM does not change.

q: What does the React Compiler do?
options: At runtime, it skips components whose props did not change
At build time, it adds memoization to components and hooks
It turns slow renders into transitions
At runtime, it deep-compares props in place of memo, so memo becomes useless
explain: The compiler is a build-time Babel plugin that rewrites components and hooks to cache values, callbacks and JSX, equivalent to memo, useMemo and useCallback, even conditionally. It does not change update priorities, and nothing in it deep-compares props at runtime.

q: The page passes useDeferredValue(query) to FilteredOrdersTable, which is not wrapped in memo. How many times does the table render for one keystroke?
options: Once, with the new query, after the input has painted
Once, with the old query only
Twice: with the old query, then with the new one
Zero times until the user stops typing, as with a debounce
explain: The urgent render renders the parent, and without memo the table renders too, with the old deferred value; then the background render runs with the new value. Measured on React 19.3.1: 2 renders without memo, 1 with it. That is why react.dev says the optimisation requires memo.

q: What does startTransition(fn) do with fn?
options: It runs fn in a Web Worker
It schedules fn to run later, when the browser reports that it is idle
It runs fn in slices of 5 ms, yielding between slices
It calls fn now and defers the state updates made in it
explain: react.dev states that the function is called immediately; only the state updates scheduled synchronously during it become transitions. So computation inside fn runs on the main thread right away (measured: 152 to 160 ms per keystroke with a 150 ms calculation inside). Slicing applies to rendering, between components, not to your callback.

q: Which is a real cost of virtualising the orders table?
options: Find-in-page cannot find orders whose rows are not rendered
Every row must be wrapped in memo, or virtualisation has no effect
The list must be sorted on the server
Only fixed row heights are supported, so long rows get truncated
explain: A virtualised list renders only the visible rows, so the rest is not in the DOM, and find-in-page, printing and "select all" only see what is rendered. TanStack Virtual handles variable heights with measureElement, and works without memo because it renders only a few dozen rows.

q: The Refunds tab is wrapped in <Activity mode="hidden"> while the agent looks at History. What is true for the hidden tab?
options: It is unmounted: its state is lost and its effects are cleaned up
Its DOM is hidden, its effects destroyed, its state kept
It keeps its effects running but stops re-rendering
Its DOM is removed and its state is saved to sessionStorage until shown
explain: A hidden Activity keeps the children's state and DOM, hides the DOM with display: none, and destroys their effects; showing it again restores the state and re-creates the effects (measured on React 19.3.1). Unmounting is what conditional rendering does, and is the cause of the lost refund note.

q: An interviewer shows this code: "OrderRow is memoized, yet the Profiler shows all rows rendering on each keystroke, with 'Props changed: (onOpen)'. Which fix would you ship?"
options: Give memo a custom comparison that ignores onOpen, since it always navigates
Remove memo: it cannot work with callback props
Deep-compare every prop in a custom comparison
Create onOpen once with useCallback, or enable the compiler
explain: The inline arrow is a new function on every render, so Object.is sees a changed prop. A stable function from useCallback fixes it, and the compiler would cache it automatically. Ignoring onOpen in a custom comparison is the tempting shortcut, but react.dev warns that the row would then keep calling a stale handler from an older render.

q: Rows are memoized and the handler stable. An order changes from paid to shipped through this live update. What does the agent see?
options: The row updates to shipped, because the array is a new reference
Every row renders again
The row still shows paid: memo sees the same order object
React throws in development, because state was mutated in place
explain: The table renders because the array is new, but each row receives the same order object as before, mutated in place, so memo skips all of them: measured, 0 row renders and a stale badge. React does not detect mutation and throws nothing. The fix is to replace the changed order with { ...order, status }.

q: After every route change, all components that read AuthContext render, although the user did not change. What is the most likely cause?
options: The value is a new object on every render of App
setCurrentUser gets a new identity on every render, which changes the value
Calling trackPage during render resets the context
Readers of a context always re-render on navigation
explain: App renders on each route change, creating a new { currentUser, setCurrentUser } object; Object.is sees a different value and every reader renders. Wrapping it in useMemo with [currentUser] fixes it, as react.dev shows. State setters are stable, so they are not the cause.

q: In a Redux back office, the orders toolbar re-renders after every dispatched action, even actions about notifications. Its code is below. What is the bug?
options: React-Redux does not support destructuring a selector result
The selector returns a new object each time, compared with ===
useSelector re-renders on every action by design, whatever the selector returns
The toolbar should read the store with useContext
explain: useSelector runs the selector after every dispatched action and re-renders when the result is not === to the previous one; a new object literal is always different. Select each field separately, use a memoized selector (Reselect) or pass shallowEqual. It does not re-render on every action when the result is stable.

q: What happens when this hook is used in a row, on React 19?
options: It works, and the row renders only when isSelected flips from one value to the other
It works, but every row renders on every store change
It fails to type-check: getSnapshot must return a primitive
React warns that the snapshot should be cached, then throws
explain: getSnapshot must return the same value while the store has not changed; a new object on each call looks like a change every time. Measured on React 19.3.1: the error "The result of getSnapshot should be cached to avoid an infinite loop", then "Maximum update depth exceeded". Objects are allowed if cached; returning the boolean itself is the simple fix.

q: Your team enables the React Compiler in an existing app full of useMemo and useCallback. A colleague opens a PR that removes all of them "since the compiler does it now". What do you answer?
options: Approve: the compiler ignores manual memoization, so the hooks are dead code
Reject: the compiler needs manual memoization to work
Keep them, or remove them with tests: removal can change the output
Approve, with 'use no memo' in every touched file
explain: react.dev recommends leaving existing memoization in place, because removing it can change compilation output, or removing it carefully with tests; effects that depend on a memoized value are the usual risk. The compiler does not ignore manual hooks, and does not need them either; in new code, it is the default and the hooks are escape hatches.

q: You introduce the React Compiler into the back office, a large Vite app with patchy tests. Which plan would you defend?
options: Turn it on everywhere with ^1.0.0, ship, and fix what agents report
Lint first, then compile part of the app, with an exact version pin
Remove every useMemo first, then enable it everywhere at once
Wait: the compiler is still experimental
explain: This is the rollout react.dev describes: the recommended config of eslint-plugin-react-hooks surfaces Rules of React violations, incremental adoption limits the blast radius, and an exact version avoids silent behaviour changes without good test coverage. The compiler has been stable since 1.0 (7 October 2025), so waiting is not justified.

q: The lint reports on the virtualised table: "Compilation Skipped: Use of incompatible library" on useVirtualizer. What does it mean?
options: The build fails until the call is removed
TanStack Virtual does not work with React 19, so the table breaks at runtime
The compiler memoizes the component anyway and warns in the browser at runtime
The compiler leaves this component unmemoized, to avoid stale UI
explain: The message is a warning: the compiler skips memoizing that component to avoid stale UI, because useVirtualizer() returns functions that cannot be memoized safely (measured with eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1). The component still works as plain React; only automatic memoization is lost there. TanStack Table and React Hook Form's watch are on the same list.

q: The compiler is enabled and the ✨ badge shows on OrdersTable, yet each keystroke still takes over 100 ms. The table filters 5,000 orders by query. Why?
options: A new query is a new input: the filter must run again
The compiler only optimises development builds, not production
The compiler never memoizes the result of Array.prototype.filter
The compiler disables concurrent rendering
explain: Memoization caches results for unchanged inputs; a new query is a new input, so the expensive part runs anyway. That is the "one render is too slow" problem, solved by deferring (useDeferredValue), rendering less (virtualisation) or computing less. The compiler targets production builds, and react.dev shows it memoizing calculations made during render, such as this filter.

q: To fix the lagging filter, a colleague writes this. What is wrong?
options: isPending is never read, so React ignores the transition
Nothing: react.dev recommends this pattern for search inputs
The input's own value must not be in a transition
startTransition must be imported from react-dom, not taken from the hook
explain: An input must update synchronously with its change event, and transitions are non-blocking, so react.dev states they cannot control text inputs. Keep query urgent and either set a second tableQuery state inside the transition or pass useDeferredValue(query) to a memoized table. Reading isPending is optional.

q: The back office has two searches: filtering the 5,000 orders already in memory, and a customer search that calls GET /customers?q=. What would you use for each?
options: useDeferredValue for both: deferring the value also limits network calls
A deferred value for the filter, a debounce for the API
A 300 ms debounce for both, to keep one pattern
A transition for the API call, nothing for the filter
explain: Deferred rendering has no fixed delay and is interruptible, which suits rendering work; it does not reduce the number of requests. react.dev notes that debouncing still helps for non-rendering work such as network calls. A debounce on the in-memory filter only postpones the moment the render blocks the keystroke.

q: "Why does wrapping an expensive calculation in startTransition still freeze typing?" Pick the best answer.
options: Transitions only work with useTransition, not the standalone function
Both updates are batched into one urgent render
React treats every update inside an event handler as urgent
The callback runs now, so rankOrders runs inside the keystroke
explain: React calls the callback right away, so the 150 ms calculation runs in the event handler before the browser can paint; measured in Chromium, each keystroke took 152 to 160 ms. The standalone startTransition marks updates exactly like the hook's, without isPending. Move the work into rendering under a deferred value, make it smaller, or move it to a worker.

q: Both versions do 150 ms of work per update in a deferred render: version A in one component's useMemo, version B split across 50 small components of 3 ms each. What did typing look like in Chromium?
options: Both were smooth: a deferred render never blocks input
Both blocked typing for about 150 ms per keystroke, since the total work is equal
A delayed keystrokes; B kept them all under 16 ms
B was worse: 50 components cost more than one
explain: React checks whether to yield between components, never inside one, so A is a single 150 ms block: measured, 150 ms long tasks and keystrokes delayed up to about 100 ms. B gives React 50 points to yield, and no keystroke exceeded 16 ms. Deferral only helps when the work is divisible.

q: Product asks for "all 50,000 orders of the year in one table, fast". What would you propose first?
options: Server-side pagination first; virtualise only if a long scroll is needed
Render all 50,000 rows with the React Compiler, which skips unchanged rows
Render all rows in one transition
Load all rows and hide off-screen ones with CSS
explain: Rendering cost grows with the number of rows in the DOM: measured, 5,000 rows took 0.6 to 3.6 s to mount against under 30 ms for a 40-row window. Pagination also cuts the data sent; virtualisation is the answer when one long scrollable list is a real need. The compiler and transitions do not reduce the work of rendering rows that change.

q: An accessibility review of the virtualised orders table says a screen reader announces "table with 30 rows". What is missing?
options: aria-busy on the table while the agent scrolls
aria-rowcount on the table and aria-rowindex on rows
A tabindex on every rendered row so it can be counted
Nothing: screen readers cannot announce the size of a virtualised list
explain: MDN says aria-rowcount is needed when not all rows are in the DOM, to give the real size of the table, and each rendered row then carries its position with aria-rowindex. Without them, assistive technology counts only the rendered rows. aria-busy signals updates in progress, not the size.

q: Where would you put Suspense boundaries on the order detail page (header, lines, refunds tab, history tab)?
options: Around every component that loads something, so each piece appears as soon as it can
One boundary around the whole app
Where the design shows loading states: the panel, the lazy tab
None: Suspense only works with Server Components
explain: Everything inside one boundary appears together, so boundaries encode the loading sequence; react.dev advises against a boundary around every component and suggests following the designers' loading states. One boundary for everything makes the slowest part hold back the page. Suspense works on the client with lazy and use too.

q: Clicking the Refunds tab, whose code is not loaded yet, replaces the whole panel with a skeleton. With startTransition(() => setTab('refunds')) instead of a plain setTab, what happens?
options: Details stays on screen, with isPending true until Refunds is ready
The skeleton still shows, but for a shorter time because the code loads in parallel
The Refunds tab renders empty, then fills in
React throws: lazy cannot load inside a transition
explain: A transition tells React not to hide already revealed content with a fallback: it keeps the Details tab and reports isPending. Measured on React 19.3.1: the plain switch showed the fallback, the transition kept Details with isPending true, then showed the form when the code arrived. Transitions do not speed up loading.

q: The History tab subscribes to live order events in an effect, and is wrapped in <Activity>. What happens to the subscription while the tab is hidden?
options: It keeps running, and the hidden tab updates in real time
It keeps running, but React buffers the events until the tab is visible again
It is cancelled, and the tab's state is reset when shown
Cleanup runs on hide, the effect re-runs on show, state is kept
explain: Hiding an Activity destroys its children's effects, which runs their cleanups, and showing it re-creates them; the state is kept throughout (measured on React 19.3.1). So the subscription stops while hidden, and the effect must refetch or resubscribe on show. State is not reset: that is the difference with conditional rendering.
